props.title: Bill Cunningham New York

sections.content: **Bill Cunningham New York (2010)** (2010) revolutionized fashion documentary filmmaking by turning the lens on one of photography's most humble yet influential figures. The film captures Cunningham's daily bicycle rides through Manhattan, photographing street fashion with the same enthusiasm he brought to high society events. This intimate portrait connects perfectly with other groundbreaking fashion documentaries like The September Issue (2009) and Iris (2014), but Cunningham's monk-like dedication to his craft and his tiny Carnegie Hall apartment set this film apart.

sections.content: What makes Cunningham's story so compelling is how it captures a vanishing New York. Like **Paris is Burning** (1990) documented the city's ballroom culture and Finding Vivian Maier (2013) uncovered a hidden street photographer, this film preserves a crucial piece of NYC cultural history. Cunningham's decades-long perch at The New York Times allowed him to chronicle both high society at charity galas and everyday people expressing themselves through fashion.

The film excels at showing how Cunningham's ascetic personal life (he slept on a cot among filing cabinets) contrasted with the glamorous world he photographed. This tension between art and commerce, between observation and participation, echoes through other great artist documentaries like **Herb & Dorothy** (2008) and **The Salt of the Earth** (2014) about photographer Sebastião Salgado. sections.content: Cunningham's influence on street photography and fashion documentation can't be overstated. His work bridged the gap between **Weegee: The Famous** (1993), who captured raw street life, and modern social media fashion influencers. The film shows how his democratic eye - treating a kid in a punk jacket with the same respect as a socialite in couture - transformed fashion photography. This approach influenced later works like **Faces Places** (2017), where photographer JR similarly celebrates ordinary people.
